intro: How an electric car and a DC fast charger talk during a charge. A DC charger feeds direct current straight into the battery. The messages travel as a powerline signal, like a home network over the power sockets, on the control pilot: a thin signal wire in the charging cable. On top run IPv6 and TCP, as on the internet. The car leads: it asks for each step and for the current it wants, and the charger answers with what it can give.
plain: When you plug an electric car into a fast charger, the car and the charger talk to each other through the cable. Before any power flows, they agree how the charge will be paid for, test that the cable is safe and share their limits. Then the car keeps telling the charger how much current its battery wants, as you would tell someone filling your glass: more, slower, stop.

plug.title: Plug in and pair
plug.text: The charger sends a square wave on the control pilot. Its duty cycle (the share of each cycle the signal stays high) is 5 %, which means: let us talk digitally. Next, the powerline modems of car and charger find each other. This is SLAC (signal level attenuation characterization): the car picks the charger that hears it best. Then the car asks everyone on the link (address ff02::1, UDP port 15118) for the charger's IP address and port. This is SDP, the discovery protocol.

session.title: Open a session
session.text: The car opens a TCP connection to the charger, then TLS, which encrypts it. The two agree on a protocol version, and the charger opens a session.

limits.title: Payment and limits
limits.text: The driver pays with a card at the charger. Car and charger tell each other their limits: voltage, current and power.

prepare.title: Check and match voltage
prepare.text: Before any current flows, the charger tests the cable's insulation: no current may leak to earth. Then it raises its voltage to the battery's. This is the pre-charge.

charge.title: Car asks for current
charge.text: The car closes its contactors (the heavy switches between battery and cable) and asks for current. It keeps asking, and the charger follows.

stop.title: Charging stops
stop.text: When the battery is 80 % full, the car ends the charge, and then the session.

frames.slac: Which charger is on my cable?
frames.sdp-req: Where are you? I want TLS over TCP
frames.tls: Prove who you are, then encrypt
frames.payment: I will pay outside the car: ExternalPayment
frames.params: I can give 500 V, 125 A, 50 kW

notes.cp: This part is still IEC 61851: a 1 kHz square wave with a 5 % duty cycle. 5 % offers no current. It means "use digital communication". The car's powerline modem wakes up.
notes.slac: SLAC (ISO 15118-3) finds the charger at the other end of this cable. In a parking lot, signals leak from one cable to the next. So the car sends a burst of sounding messages, and every charger that hears them reports how strong they arrived. The car picks the strongest with CM_SLAC_MATCH.REQ. That charger answers CM_SLAC_MATCH.CNF with the key of a private powerline network for the two of them.
notes.tls: The car opens TCP to [fe80::ff:fe00:a1]:54321, then TLS 1.2. The charger shows its certificate. The car checks it against the V2G root certificates it holds: the trusted signers of charger certificates. From here on, everything is encrypted.
notes.app: The first message in the session lists the protocols the car speaks, each with a version and a priority. The charger answers supportedAppProtocolRes with OK_SuccessfulNegotiation and the SchemaID it picked: 1, ISO 15118-2. The playground shows the message as XML.
notes.setup: The car sent SessionSetupReq with its EVCCID: the MAC address (hardware address) of its modem, 02-00-00-00-00-E1. The charger answers with a new 8-byte SessionID, its EVSEID and the time. Every message after this one carries the SessionID in its header.
notes.payment: Before this came ServiceDiscovery. The charger offered DC charging and two ways to pay: Contract (Plug & Charge, where the car pays by itself) and ExternalPayment. The car picks ExternalPayment: the driver pays with a card or an app. Then the car repeats AuthorizationReq until the charger answers Finished.
notes.params: The car sent its limits and its state of charge (how full the battery is), 54 %. The charger answers with its own: at most 500 V, 125 A and 50 kW. Each value is a 16-bit whole number, a power of ten and a unit. So 50 kW travels as 5000 × 10^1 W.
notes.cable-check: The car has set the control pilot to state C: ready to charge. The charger puts a test voltage on the DC cable and measures the insulation to earth. It answers Ongoing until it is done, then Finished, with EVSEIsolationStatus Valid.
notes.pre-charge: The battery is at 396 V, behind the car's open contactors. The car asks the charger to raise its output to the same voltage, with at most 2 A. The charger answers with its present voltage, 395 V: close enough to close the contactors without a spark.
notes.power-on: The car has closed its contactors. ChargeProgress Start: from now on the charger may deliver current.
notes.current-demand: The car asks for 120 A, with its state of charge. It sends the next request as soon as the answer arrives. The charger answers each one with what it delivers: 398 V, 120 A. The car is in control: it changes the current as the battery fills.
notes.stop: First comes PowerDeliveryReq with ChargeProgress Stop: the current falls to 0 and the car opens its contactors. WeldingDetection checks that they really opened and did not weld shut. Then SessionStopReq with ChargingSession Terminate ends the session.

version.name: V2GTP version
version.note: Version 0x01, then the same byte with every bit inverted, 0xFE. A receiver drops a message with anything else here.

sdp-req.name: Payload type
sdp-req.note: 0x9000: an SDP request, asking where the charger is.

sdp-res.name: Payload type
sdp-res.note: 0x9001: an SDP response, saying where the charger is.

len-2.name: Length
len-2.note: 2 bytes of payload follow. The header itself is always 8 bytes.

len-20.name: Length
len-20.note: 0x14 = 20 bytes follow: address, port, security and transport.

tls-req.name: Security
tls-req.note: 0x00: the car wants TLS, an encrypted connection. 0x10 would mean without TLS.

ip-prefix.name: IPv6 prefix
ip-prefix.note: fe80::/64: a link-local address. It is valid only on this link, the private powerline network of car and charger.

ip-id.name: Interface ID
ip-id.note: Made from the charger's MAC address, 02-00-00-00-00-A1: FF FE goes in the middle, and the 0x02 bit is flipped. The whole address is fe80::ff:fe00:a1.

port.name: TCP port
port.note: 0xD431 = 54321: where the charger waits for this car.

a-urn.name: URN
a-urn.note: A uniform resource name: a fixed label, not an address to open.

a-body.name: Body
a-body.note: iso: the organization that owns the name.

a-standard.name: Standard
a-standard.note: 15118: communication between a vehicle and the grid.

a-part.name: Part
a-part.note: Part 2: the network and application messages.

a-year.name: Year
a-year.note: 2013, the date in the schema's name. The standard itself came out in 2014.

a-schema.name: Schema
a-schema.note: MsgDef: the message definitions. DIN 70121 uses urn:din:70121:2012:MsgDef.

facts.standard: ISO 15118-2 (2014) for the messages, ISO 15118-3 for the powerline. ISO 15118-20 is the next generation.
facts.between: The car's communication controller (EVCC) → the charger's (SECC). The car asks, the charger answers.
facts.transport: HomePlug Green PHY on the control pilot, IPv6, SDP on UDP 15118, then TCP
facts.security: TLS 1.2: the charger proves itself with a certificate. Plug & Charge adds a contract certificate in the car, so the car can pay by itself.
facts.frames: EXI (XML packed into bits) inside an 8-byte V2GTP header

tips: Many failed charges never get past SLAC. Check the modem, the control pilot wiring and the signal strength the charger reports before you look at messages.
Every physical value is an integer, a power of ten and a unit. Read the Multiplier: 5000 with Multiplier 1 is 50 kW, not 5 kW.
Slow work, like CableCheck or Authorization, is answered at once with EVSEProcessing Ongoing, and the car asks again. A charger that holds back its answer instead makes the car give up.
Many chargers still pick DIN 70121 from the car's list. A capture where urn:din:70121:2012:MsgDef is chosen explains why Plug & Charge never starts.

anatomy.namespace: The name of a protocol version, as supportedAppProtocol carries it

playground.file: The car's first message in the session, written as XML. On the wire it travels as EXI, which packs the same content into a few dozen bytes.
playground.root: The root element, which holds all the others. Its own namespace, from 2010, is the same in every version, so any charger can read this first message.
playground.version: Version 2.0. A charger with another minor version may answer OK_SuccessfulNegotiationWithMinorDeviation.
playground.schema-id: A number the car gives this entry. The charger names its choice by it.
playground.din: Second entry: DIN 70121, the older DC protocol. It has no TLS and no Plug & Charge.
